<document>
<title>Eiffel Tower</title>
<fragment>
The design of the Eiffel Tower is attributed to Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, two senior engineers working for the Compagnie des Établissements Eiffel. It was envisioned after discussion about a suitable centerpiece for the proposed 1889 Exposition Universelle, a world's fair to celebrate the centennial of the French Revolution. Eiffel openly acknowledged that inspiration for a tower came from the Latting Observatory built in New York City in 1853.[8] In May 1884, working at home, Koechlin made a sketch of their idea, described by him as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal trusses at regular intervals".[9] Eiffel initially showed little enthusiasm, but he did approve further study, and the two engineers then asked Stephen Sauvestre, the head of the company's architectural department, to contribute to the design. 
</fragment>
</document>

<document>
<title>Gustave Eiffel</title>
<fragment>
The design of the Eiffel Tower was originated by Maurice Koechlin and Emile Nouguier, who had discussed ideas for a centrepiece for the 1889 Exposition Universelle. In May 1884 Koechlin, working at his home, made an outline drawing of their scheme, described by him as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal trusses at regular intervals".[23] Initially Eiffel showed little enthusiasm, although he did sanction further study of the project, and the two engineers then asked Stephen Sauvestre to add architectural embellishments. Sauvestre added the decorative arches to the base, a glass pavilion to the first level and the cupola at the top. The enhanced idea gained Eiffel's support for the project, and he bought the rights to the patent on the design which Koechlin, Nougier and Sauvestre had taken out. 
</fragment>
</document>

In 1957, Utzon unexpectedly won the competition to design the Sydney Opera House. His submission was one of 233 designs from 32 countries, many of them from the most famous architects of the time.[9] Although he had won six other architectural competitions previously, the Opera House was his first non-domestic project. One of the judges, Eero Saarinen, described it as "genius" and declared he could not endorse any other choice.[10]

Other craftsmen were necessary for the building of the Parthenon, specifically carpenters and metalworkers. Unskilled labourers also had key roles in the building of the Parthenon. They loaded and unloaded the marble blocks and moved the blocks from place to place. In order to complete a project like the Parthenon, many different labourers were needed.[62]

In the mid-5th century BC, when the Athenian Acropolis became the seat of the Delian League and Athens was the greatest cultural centre of its time, Pericles initiated an ambitious building project that lasted the entire second half of the century. The most important buildings visible on the Acropolis today – the Parthenon, the Propylaia, the Erechtheion and the temple of Athena Nike – were erected during this period. The Parthenon was built under the general supervision of Phidias, who also had charge of the sculptural decoration. The architects Ictinos and Callicrates began their work in 447, and the building was substantially completed by 432. Work on the decorations continued until at least 431.[*citation needed*]

Its decorative sculptures are considered some of the high points of classical Greek art, an enduring symbol of Ancient Greece, democracy and Western civilization.[8][9]


The Parthenon was built in thanksgiving for the Hellenic victory over Persian Empire invaders during the Greco-Persian Wars.[10] Like most Greek temples, the Parthenon also served as the city treasury.[11][12]

<document>
<title>Ictinus</title>
<fragment>
Mid-5th-century BC Athenian architect

This article is about the arcitect. For the mythological character, see Ictinus (mythology).

**Ictinus** (/ɪkˈtaɪnəs/; Template:Lang-el, *Iktinos*) was an architect active in the mid 5th century BC.[1][2] Ancient sources identify Ictinus and Callicrates as co-architects of the Parthenon. He co-wrote a book on the project – which is now lost – in collaboration with Carpion.[3]


Pausanias identifies Ictinus as architect of the Temple of Apollo at Bassae.[3] That temple was Doric on the exterior, Ionic on the interior, and incorporated a Corinthian column, the earliest known, at the center rear of the cella. Sources also identify Ictinus as architect of the Telesterion at Eleusis, a gigantic hall used in the Eleusinian Mysteries.[4]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Pericles also commissioned Ictinus to design the Telesterion (Hall of mystery
) at Eleusis, but his involvement was terminated when Pericles fell from power. Three other architects took over instead.[3] It seems likely that Ictinus's reputation was harmed by his links with the fallen ruler, as he is singled out for condemnation by Aristophanes in his play *The Birds*, dated to around 414 BC. It depicts the royal kite or *ictinus* – a play on the architect's name – not as a noble bird of prey but as a scavenger stealing sacrifices from the gods and money from men. As no other classical author describes the bird in this fashion, Aristophanes likely intended it to be a dig at the architect.[5]


The artist Jean Auguste Dominique Ingres painted a scene showing Ictinus together with the lyric poet Pindar. The painting is known as *Pindar and Ictinus* and is exhibited at the National Gallery, London.

<document>
<title>Callicrates</title>
<content>
5th-century BC Greek architect

This article is about the ancient Greek architect. For other uses, see Callicrates (disambiguation).

**Callicrates** or **Kallikrates** (/kəˈlɪkrəˌtiːz/; Template:Lang-el Template:IPA-el) was an ancient Greek architect active in the middle of the fifth century BC. He and Ictinus were architects of the Parthenon (Plutarch, *Pericles*, 13).[1] An inscription identifies him as the architect of "the Temple of Nike" on the Acropolis of Athens (IG I3 35). The temple in question is either the amphiprostyle Temple of Athena Nike now visible on the site[2] or a small-scale predecessor (naiskos) whose remains were found in the later temple's foundations.[3]


An inscription identifies Callicrates as one of the architects of the Classical circuit wall of the Acropolis (IG I3 45), and Plutarch further states (loc. cit.) that he was contracted to build the middle of three defensive walls linking Athens and Piraeus.


A crater on the planet Mercury was named in his honor.[4]

<document>
<title>Phidias</title>
<fragment>

![](image)*Phidias Showing the Frieze of the Parthenon to his Friends* (1868) by Sir Lawrence Alma-Tadema
**Phidias** or **Pheidias** (/ˈf/, *Pheidias*; c. 480 – 430 BC) was an Ancient Greek sculptor, painter, and architect, active in the 5th century BC. His Statue of Zeus at Olympia was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Phidias also designed the statues of the goddess Athena on the Athenian Acropolis, namely the *Athena Parthenos* inside the Parthenon, and the *Athena Promachos*, a colossal bronze which stood between it and the Propylaea,[1] a monumental gateway that served as the entrance to the Acropolis in Athens. Phidias was the son of Charmides of Athens.[2] The ancients believed that his masters were Hegias[3] and Ageladas.[4][*better source needed*]


</fragment>
<fragment>

In 447 BC, Pericles commissioned several sculptures for Athens from Phidias to celebrate the Greek victory against the Persians at the Battle of Marathon during the Greco-Persian Wars (490 BC). Pericles used some of the money from the maritime League of Delos,[8] to rebuild and decorate Athens to celebrate this victory. Inscriptions prove that the marble blocks intended for the pedimental statues of the Parthenon were not brought to Athens until 434 BC.[*citation needed*] It is therefore possible that most of sculptural decoration of the Parthenon was the work of Phidias' workshop including pupils of Phidias, such as Alcamenes and Agoracritus.[*citation needed*]

The earliest of Phidias' works were dedications in memory of Marathon, celebrating the Greek victory. His first commission was a group of national heroes with Miltiades as a central figure. At Delphi he created a great group in bronze including the figures of Greek gods Apollo and Athena, several Attic heroes, and General Miltiades the Younger. On the Acropolis of Athens, Phidias constructed a colossal bronze statue of Athena, the *Athena Promachos*, which was visible far out at sea. Athena was the goddess of wisdom and warriors and the protector of Athens. At Pellene in Achaea, and at Plataea, Phidias made two other statues of Athena, as well as a statue of the goddess Aphrodite in ivory and gold for the people of Elis.

Based on my research of the Wikipedia articles on the Parthenon and its key figures, here's comprehensive information about the architects and their roles in building the Parthenon:

## Key Figures in the Parthenon's Construction

### **Phidias - General Supervisor and Sculptural Director**
- **Role**: Phidias served as the **general supervisor** of the entire Parthenon building project under Pericles' patronage
- **Primary Responsibilities**: 
  - Overall artistic direction and supervision of the temple's construction
  - **Charge of all sculptural decoration** throughout the building
  - Designed the famous **Athena Parthenos** statue that stood inside the temple
  - Also created the **Athena Promachos**, a monumental bronze statue on the Acropolis

### **Iktinos (Ictinus) - Co-Architect**
- **Role**: One of the two principal architects who designed the Parthenon
- **Collaboration**: Worked jointly with Callicrates on the architectural design
- **Other Major Works**: 
  - Temple of Apollo at Bassae (notable for being the first temple to incorporate all three Greek orders: Doric, Ionic, and Corinthian)
  - Temple of Telesterion at Eleusis
- **Additional Details**: Co-wrote a book (now lost) about the Parthenon project with Carpion

### **Kallikrates (Callicrates) - Co-Architect**
- **Role**: The other principal architect who collaborated with Iktinos
- **Additional Major Works**:
  - Architect of the **Temple of Athena Nike** on the Acropolis
  - Designed portions of the **Classical circuit wall** of the Acropolis
  - Built defensive walls linking Athens and Piraeus

## Timeline and Collaboration Details

- **Construction Period**: Work began in **447 BC** and the building was substantially completed by **432 BC**
- **Decorative Work**: Continued until at least **431 BC**
- **Patron**: The entire project was initiated by **Pericles** as part of his ambitious building program to celebrate Athens' victory over the Persian Empire

## Architectural Achievement

The collaboration between these three figures created what is considered:
- One of the greatest achievements of classical Greek architecture
- An enduring symbol of Ancient Greece, democracy, and Western civilization
- The high point of classical Greek art, particularly in its decorative sculptures

The division of responsibilities was clear: **Iktinos and Kallikrates** handled the architectural design and structural elements, while **Phidias** provided the artistic vision and supervised all sculptural work, ensuring aesthetic unity across this monumental project.

Based on my research, here are the architects and designers for each of your five famous historical landmarks:

## **1. Eiffel Tower**
**Primary Architects/Designers:**
- **Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier** - Senior engineers who originated the structural design in May 1884. They created the original concept described as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal trusses at regular intervals."
- **Stephen Sauvestre** - Head of the architectural department who added the decorative elements including the arches at the base, glass pavilion on the first level, and cupola at the top.
- **Gustave Eiffel** - Project lead and promoter who initially showed little enthusiasm but eventually bought the rights to the patent and supervised construction.

## **2. Sydney Opera House**
**Primary Architect:**
- **Jørn Utzon** - Danish architect who won the 1957 international competition with his design, selected from 233 submissions from 32 countries. Judge Eero Saarinen described his submission as "genius." This was Utzon's first non-domestic project.

## **3. Taj Mahal**
**Primary Architect:**
- **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** - The principal architect of the Taj Mahal under Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan. He is credited with designing the entire complex and was also known as "Nadir-ul-Asar Ahmad Mimar Lahori Shahjehani." (Note: While there are various theories about other potential architects like Ustad Isa or European designers, Lahori is most consistently credited in historical records.)

## **4. Empire State Building**
**Primary Architect:**
- **William F. Lamb** - The principal designer of the Empire State Building, working for the architectural firm Shreve, Lamb & Harmon. Lamb created the building's design in just two weeks, drawing inspiration from earlier skyscrapers like the Reynolds Building in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

## **5. Parthenon**
**Primary Architects/Designers:**
- **Iktinos (Ictinus)** and **Kallikrates (Callicrates)** - The two principal architects who collaborated on the structural design of the Parthenon (447-432 BC). Iktinos also designed the Temple of Apollo at Bassae, while Kallikrates designed the Temple of Athena Nike on the Acropolis.
- **Phidias** - General supervisor of the entire project and director of all sculptural decoration. He created the famous Athena Parthenos statue inside the temple and the Athena Promachos on the Acropolis.

Each of these landmarks represents remarkable collaborative efforts between multiple talented individuals, though some like the Sydney Opera House had a single visionary architect, while others like the Parthenon and Eiffel Tower involved teamwork between structural engineers, architects, and artistic directors.
